findings: No sustained arrhythmia. No pauses greater than 2 seconds. No AV block.

csf.interpretation: Unremarkable CSF. Normal cell count, protein, and glucose.

ct.impression: No acute intracranial abnormality. No haemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus, or large-territory infarct.

findings: Normal sinus rhythm. Normal axis and intervals. No acute ST-T changes.
Trace physiological mitral regurgitation. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.
echo.impression: Structurally normal heart; trace physiological mitral regurgitation.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Right Hoover sign, dragging gait, variable arm power and entraining tremor; hemisensory loss supportive only
action_criteria.label: Examine for positive functional signs
action_criteria.rationale: The right-sided weakness and tremor are diagnosed at the bedside: Hoover sign, dragging gait, variability and tremor entrainment are signs of clinical incompatibility (DSM-5 criterion B; Daum 2014).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal sodium, calcium, glucose, magnesium and thiamine; only GGT is raised
action_criteria.label: Electrolytes, magnesium and thiamine
action_criteria.rationale: Daily drinking with episodes of unresponsiveness raises a metabolic or withdrawal contribution; a metabolic panel with magnesium and thiamine answers that named question once.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No structural lesion to account for the right-sided deficit
action_criteria.label: Non-contrast brain MRI
action_criteria.rationale: A right-sided deficit progressing over 3 months after a blast injury makes one scan defensible, but the positive signs have already made the diagnosis (Espay 2018).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Sinus rhythm with normal conduction and QT interval
action_criteria.label: 12-lead ECG
action_criteria.rationale: Episodes of apparent unresponsiveness: NICE advises a 12-lead ECG after transient loss of consciousness (CG109) and after a suspected seizure (NG217). The event semiology already favours functional seizures, so it does not contribute to the diagnosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Habitual events recorded on video with no EEG change and a normal interictal record
action_criteria.label: Video-EEG to capture a habitual event
action_criteria.rationale: A blast injury and daily alcohol raise post-traumatic and withdrawal seizures, so a habitual event recorded without ictal change, which reaches the ILAE documented level, is the clearest answer, and co-occurring epilepsy is assessed before any antiseizure decision (LaFrance 2013; AAN 2025). Without the recording, the positive signs and the semiology of witnessed events support the diagnosis at a lower ILAE level of certainty (LaFrance 2013).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: SSRI and NSAID bleeding risk, increased by alcohol
action_criteria.label: Review the medication list
action_criteria.rationale: Sertraline with ibuprofen is a bleeding-risk pair worth noting, but no antiseizure drug or benzodiazepine is prescribed and nothing in the list changes the diagnosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Quantifies mood, anxiety and symptom burden to guide therapy; does not make the diagnosis
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological assessment of the comorbidity
action_criteria.rationale: PTSD, alcohol use and the mild TBI history are treatment targets; a battery can characterize them but does not make the diagnosis (Espay 2018).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on positive signs and treatment trials in FND
action_criteria.label: Search the literature on FND diagnosis and treatment
action_criteria.rationale: Background reading only; the diagnosis and the plan rest on this patient's examination and recorded data, not on a search.

prohibited_recommendations: Order further investigations once the positive diagnosis is established, without a new specific clinical question (repeat MRI, CT, lumbar puncture, EMG or nerve conduction studies, evoked potentials, PET).
Tell the patient the symptoms are imagined, feigned, 'all in your head', or that nothing is wrong.
Perform invasive testing without a specific indication (lumbar puncture, nerve or muscle biopsy, catheter angiography).
Start or escalate antiseizure medication for the functional seizures.
Give benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.
Give gadolinium contrast without a specific indication.
required_recommendations: Make a positive diagnosis of functional neurological disorder (mixed: functional seizures with functional right-sided weakness and tremor) based on the right Hoover sign, dragging gait, variability of arm strength and tremor entrainment and the semiology of the habitual episodes, confirmed on video-EEG where recorded, and not by exclusion of other disease.

Explain the diagnosis to the patient, and with consent to the family, as a common and genuine disorder of nervous system functioning that can improve, show the positive signs, and give written information.
Refer for physiotherapy with expertise in functional motor disorder (motor retraining, Nielsen 2015 consensus).
Refer for psychological therapy by a clinician experienced in FND (CBT-informed) and treat the comorbid PTSD with trauma-focused psychological therapy.

Give the patient, family and ward a written plan for typical events: keep safe, do not restrain, wait for the event to end, and do not give emergency benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.
Assess alcohol use and offer a brief intervention.

avoided_actions.rationale: No murmur, embolic or structural cardiac question in a 31-year-old with functional weakness and events.
The episodes are not syncopal; rhythm monitoring answers no question here.
The blast injury was in 2019 and there is no new head injury; a CT adds radiation and answers no question the examination has not.
No fever, meningism or encephalopathy; a lumbar puncture is invasive and answers no question.
PET has no role in functional weakness or functional seizures, including after mild TBI.
Reflexes are normal and the weakness has positive functional signs; nerve conduction studies and EMG answer no question and a normal study reinforces the search for an organic cause.
A non-anatomical hemibody sensory loss is not a somatosensory pathway question; evoked potentials add nothing.

accepted: Functional neurological disorder — right-sided functional hemimotor syndrome and PNES, with comorbid PTSD and alcohol use disorder

differential.key_features: The 2019 blast mild TBI raises post-traumatic epilepsy, although mild TBI adds little risk, and the episodes are motionless unresponsiveness with eyes closed and immediate recovery. Habitual events recorded on video-EEG without ictal change; co-occurring epilepsy remains possible in about one in five patients with functional seizures.

He drinks 2-4 beers daily, but withdrawal seizures are generalized tonic-clonic events within 1-2 days of stopping; his episodes are motionless, have recurred over 3 months while he continues to drink daily, show no withdrawal signs, and the recorded event has no ictal change.

differential.diagnosis: Structural brain lesion (chronic subdural hematoma, tumor)
differential.key_features: A right-sided deficit progressing over 3 months after a head injury raises a structural lesion, but the Hoover sign, variability, entraining tremor and normal reflexes and plantar responses are incompatible with one.

Feigning is conscious and cannot be separated from FND by examination signs; the denied VA disability claim and pending appeal are noted, and the symptoms began as the claim process intensified, so timing does not separate them, but nothing in the case suggests deliberate deception and he is distressed by symptoms that arose in the setting of long-standing combat PTSD.

key_clinical_evidence: Positive signs of functional weakness and tremor on the right: Hoover sign, dragging monoplegic gait that normalizes with distraction, arm strength varying between 2/5 and 4/5 with instructions, and a variable-frequency tremor that entrains; the non-anatomical hemibody sensory loss is supportive only.
The witnessed and ward-observed episodes are 1-2 minutes of motionless unresponsiveness with eyes closed and immediate recovery, a semiology typical of functional seizures.
Video-EEG recorded one habitual episode, confirmed as typical by his partner, with a persistent posterior rhythm and no ictal change; the interictal record is normal.
Electrolytes, glucose, calcium, magnesium and thiamine are normal and the blood alcohol is zero; GGT 88 U/L reflects his drinking. A normal post-event prolactin excludes nothing.
Combat PTSD, the 2019 mild TBI, daily alcohol and the denied disability claim are context and treatment targets; none makes or excludes the diagnosis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Mild TBI does not explain a deficit with positive functional signs and adds little epilepsy risk; the semiology decides, and an episode recorded without ictal change confirms it.
red_herrings.data_point: Mild TBI after blast exposure in 2019
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attributing the deficits to TBI sequelae or the episodes to post-traumatic epilepsy and starting antiseizure medication

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Examination signs cannot separate feigning from FND; the diagnosis rests on the positive signs and the event semiology and is explained without judgment.
red_herrings.data_point: VA disability claim denied 6 weeks ago, with an appeal hearing pending
red_herrings.intended_effect: Labelling the presentation malingering, or telling him the symptoms are put on

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The episodes are motionless, not convulsive, and recur while he continues to drink daily; the drinking is a comorbidity to address with a brief intervention.
red_herrings.data_point: 2-4 beers daily with a raised GGT
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attributing the episodes to alcohol withdrawal seizures

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: PTSD is common in FND but neither necessary nor sufficient; it is a treatment target.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Treating PTSD as proof of FND and skipping the examination and the event recording

findings.result: Right hip extension weak on direct testing, full strength during contralateral left hip flexion against resistance.
Right leg dragged behind with the foot kept on the floor; the gait normalizes with distraction.
Right arm strength varies between 2/5 and 4/5 with different instructions.
Right hand tremor of variable frequency (4-8 Hz) takes up the examiner's tapping rhythm.
Right hemibody pinprick loss that follows no dermatomal or peripheral nerve distribution; not counted as a rule-in sign.
Ward episode of 90 seconds: eyes closed, motionless, unresponsive to voice, immediate recovery without confusion.

clinical_assessment.impression: Positive signs of functional weakness and tremor: right Hoover sign, dragging monoplegic gait, variability of right arm strength and tremor entrainment. The pattern is inconsistent with a structural lesion. The event semiology (eyes closed, motionless unresponsiveness for 90 seconds, immediate recovery) is typical of functional seizures; the examination does not by itself exclude epileptic seizures.

interactions: Sertraline with ibuprofen: increased risk of upper gastrointestinal bleeding (SSRI platelet effect with NSAID mucosal injury), higher with daily alcohol; limit NSAID use or add gastroprotection.
general.proposed: Prazosin 2 mg at bedtime; Sertraline 100 mg once daily; Ibuprofen 400 mg as needed, up to 3 times daily
general.summary: One bleeding-risk interaction (sertraline with ibuprofen), increased by daily alcohol; prazosin carries an orthostatic caution.
warnings: Prazosin: orthostatic hypotension and syncope, most often after the first dose or a dose increase; additive with alcohol.
Daily alcohol adds to the sedative effects of sertraline.

artifacts.description: Intermittent temporal muscle artifact during the event

background.description: Symmetric 10 Hz posterior dominant rhythm, reactive to eye opening. Normal sleep architecture.
background.recording: 48-hour inpatient video-EEG, wake and sleep, 10-20 electrode placement

findings.morphology: Day 2, 09:20, duration 1 min 52 s: sitting in bed, eyes closed, motionless and not responsive to voice, with immediate return to normal conversation afterwards; his partner confirmed on video review that the episode was typical. A 10 Hz posterior dominant rhythm was present throughout the event, with intermittent temporal muscle artifact from jaw and neck tension; no rhythmic evolution, no attenuation, no postictal slowing.

eeg.impression: This is a NORMAL video-EEG. One habitual event was recorded (motionless unresponsiveness with eyes closed, lasting 1 min 52 s) without ictal EEG change before, during or after the event; the posterior dominant rhythm persisted during the event. No interictal epileptiform discharges. No electrographic seizures.

labs.interpretation: GGT 88 U/L (elevated). Remaining values within reference ranges.

results.finding: Diagnosis of functional neurological disorder rests on positive clinical features such as the Hoover sign, tremor entrainment and functional seizure semiology, not on the exclusion of other disease; treatment combines explanation, physiotherapy and psychological therapy.
results.source: Espay AJ et al. JAMA Neurol 2018;75:1132-1141

results.finding: Motor signs such as the Hoover sign, hip abductor sign, drift without pronation and dragging gait have high specificity; sensory signs such as midline splitting have low specificity.
results.source: Daum C et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2014;85:180-190

results.finding: Defines levels of certainty for psychogenic nonepileptic seizures; the documented level requires a typical event recorded on video-EEG without ictal EEG change.
results.source: LaFrance WC Jr et al. Epilepsia 2013;54:2005-2018

results.finding: For functional seizures: assess for co-occurring epilepsy and psychiatric disorders, taper antiseizure medication without another indication, avoid benzodiazepines, and offer psychological therapy, which is possibly effective.
CBT added to standardised medical care did not reduce dissociative seizure frequency at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured CBT.
results.source: Goldstein LH et al. Lancet Psychiatry 2020;7:491-505

results.finding: Specialist physiotherapy for functional motor disorder was not superior to community neurological physiotherapy on physical function at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured it.
results.source: Nielsen G et al. Lancet Neurol 2024;23:675-686

results.finding: About 4% of patients diagnosed with conversion symptoms since 1970 later received another diagnosis.

functional neurological disorder diagnos.summary: Guideline and trial evidence supports a positive clinical diagnosis of functional neurological disorder, video-EEG confirmation of functional seizures, tapering of unneeded antiseizure drugs and benzodiazepines, and physiotherapy and psychological treatment whose trial effects on primary outcomes were modest.

metadata.difficulty_rationale: Clear positive signs and typical motionless unresponsive episodes, with three prompts to over-investigate or mislabel (blast TBI, daily alcohol, a denied disability claim); the work-up is the examination and a targeted metabolic panel, with a video-EEG capture to confirm the episodes if needed.
metadata.notes: Straightforward FND in a veteran with combat PTSD, remote mild TBI and daily alcohol: functional right-sided weakness and tremor with functional unresponsive episodes. FND and PTSD co-occur and are both valid diagnoses.
metadata.revision_reason: October 2026 review round: criteria rebuilt to the pack tiers (exam required, targeted labs recommended, brain MRI optional), canonical literature and medication outputs, disguised follow-ups removed, case-specific differential, evidence and assessment. Close-out 24 Oct 2026: video-EEG optional and red-flag tests recommended, per the July 2026 agreement with the physicians that the examination is the only required diagnostic act.

patient.chief_complaint: Right-sided weakness, tremor, and episodes of unresponsiveness — 3 months

medications.frequency: as needed, up to 3 times daily

past_medical_history: Post-traumatic stress disorder (combat-related, 3 tours of duty)
Mild TBI (diagnosed after blast exposure in 2019)

social_history.occupation: Veteran, currently unemployed — applying for VA disability
social_history.recent_stressor: VA disability claim denial 6 weeks ago; court hearing for disability appeal upcoming

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. K is a 31-year-old veteran with combat-related PTSD who presents with a 3-month history of progressive right-sided weakness, right hand tremor, and episodes of unresponsiveness. He served three tours of duty in the Middle East and experienced a blast exposure in 2019 for which he was diagnosed with mild traumatic brain injury. He has been applying for VA disability benefits and his claim was denied 6 weeks ago, which he finds devastating. He is appealing the decision. His neurological symptoms first appeared approximately 3 months ago, shortly after the disability claim process intensified. He initially attributed his symptoms to sequelae of his mild TBI. The episodes of unresponsiveness have been witnessed by his partner: lasting 1-2 minutes, with closed eyes, no limb movements, and immediate full recovery. He has no prior history of seizures. His PTSD symptoms include nightmares, hypervigilance, avoidance, and emotional numbing. He drinks 2-4 beers daily. He acknowledges that his symptoms cause him distress but is resistant to considering a psychological explanation, feeling that this would invalidate his disability claim.

neurological_exam.additional: Right hand tremor of variable frequency (4-8 Hz) that entrains to the examiner's tapping rhythm. One episode on the ward: 90 seconds, eyes closed, motionless, not responsive to voice, immediate recovery without confusion.
neurological_exam.gait: Drags the right leg behind with the foot kept on the floor; the gait normalizes when he is distracted by conversation.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4. Guarded and hypervigilant. Reports feeling 'checked out' at times.
neurological_exam.motor: Right arm 2/5 on formal testing, varying between 2/5 and 4/5 with different instructions. Right hip extension weak on direct testing; Hoover sign positive: right hip extension returns to full strength during contralateral left hip flexion against resistance. Left side 5/5.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Normal 2+ symmetric throughout. No pathological reflexes.
neurological_exam.sensory: Right hemibody loss to pinprick that follows no dermatomal or peripheral nerve distribution. Vibration intact throughout.
